title: Neural Authorship Attribution: Stylometric Analysis on Large Language Models
extended_summary:
This paper examines the problem of neural authorship attribution: identifying which large language model generated a given piece of text. The authors are motivated by concerns about AI-generated misinformation and argue that forensic methods are needed not only to detect machine-written text, but also to attribute it to specific source models. A central question is whether proprietary LLMs and open-source LLMs exhibit distinct writing signatures that can be measured and used for attribution.

To study this, the authors generated a corpus of 6,000 AI-written news articles using six large language models: GPT-4, GPT-3.5, Llama 1, Llama 2, and GPT-NeoX. They prompted each model with 1,000 human-authored news headlines sampled from CNN and the Washington Post source data, using generation settings of top-p = 0.9 and temperature = 0.8. They extracted 60 stylometric features spanning lexical, syntactic, and structural properties of the generated texts, and compared several classification approaches, including XGBoost with bag-of-words or stylometric features, RoBERTa-based models, and a fusion model combining RoBERTa embeddings with stylometric features.

The study does not involve educational participants, schools, or writing instruction contexts; instead, it is a computational analysis of AI-generated news text. The empirical context is a machine-generated text corpus rather than a human population. Results showed clear separation between proprietary and open-source LLM outputs, especially when stylometric features were used. The best-performing fusion model achieved near-perfect initial attribution between proprietary and open-source classes, and also outperformed alternatives for within-category attribution.

The main conclusion is that stylometric analysis provides interpretable and effective signals for attributing AI-generated text to its source LLM. Lexical diversity, parts-of-speech usage, punctuation, and paragraph structure were especially informative. The authors also conclude that attribution within open-source models is harder because some models have overlapping writing styles, although Llama 2 appeared more distinct and closer in style to proprietary models. Overall, the paper contributes a forensic methodology for analyzing LLM writing signatures rather than an educational intervention or K-12 writing outcomes study.
quality_tier_rationale: This is an arXiv preprint focused on neural authorship attribution and stylometric analysis of AI-generated news articles, not a K-12 education intervention study. It does not evaluate any educational use of AI, student sample, classroom implementation, or learning-related causal design.
impact_tier_rationale: The paper reports strong technical classification performance for attributing LLM-generated text, but it does not measure educational outcomes or intervention effects in learners. Educational impact is therefore unclear and not directly assessable within the K-12 evidence framework.
